problems.nature: phishing and social engineering via deceptive email content
problems.description: This problem involves detecting phishing and social engineering attacks embedded within email content. Attackers craft emails that leverage financial scams, fake job offers, and online pharmacy promotions, often using obfuscated URLs and impersonation of trusted institutions to deceive recipients. The detection challenge is moderate to high due to the text-heavy nature of emails, varied linguistic styles, and the use of social engineering tactics appealing to urgency and emotion. Attackers exploit multi-source datasets and balanced class distributions to evade simplistic detection, embedding narrative-rich content and suspicious metadata such as free email contacts and uncommon domain URLs.
attack_vectors: email phishing via deceptive email content
malicious URLs directing to fraudulent or malicious websites

real_world_context.domain_insights: Phishing emails often contain suspicious URLs unrelated to sender domains, urgent or lucrative subject lines, financial or personal gain narratives, and obfuscated domain names. Attackers impersonate trusted entities like banks and pharmacies, embedding contact info with free or suspicious domains to build false legitimacy.
real_world_context.attack_sophistication: Moderate sophistication with social engineering, URL obfuscation, and narrative complexity, but lacking advanced polymorphic or encrypted payloads.
real_world_context.technical_implementation: Emails include long narrative bodies exceeding 500 words describing scams, use of shortened or uncommon TLD URLs, and subject lines with monetary inducements. Contact information often uses free email providers, and attackers embed misspellings and unusual formatting to evade filters.
real_world_context.threat_landscape: Phishing exploiting financial scams and online pharmacy promotions remains prevalent. Emerging patterns include narrative-rich scam emails and diversification into health and employment themes, blending multi-source data to evade detection.
real_world_context.victim_impact: Victims risk financial loss, identity theft, and exposure to fraudulent services. Emotional manipulation and urgency increase the likelihood of engagement and compromise.

attack_signatures: Emails containing financial scams referencing large abandoned sums with detailed backstories and requests for cooperation
Phishing emails promoting online pharmacies with direct URLs and claims of FDA approval or discounts
Short, spam-like bodies with lists of cheap medications and embedded suspicious URLs
indicators_of_compromise: URLs with uncommon or newly registered domains containing numeric or random strings
Subject lines with monetary amounts or urgent calls to action
Email bodies exceeding 500 words with narrative scams including personal names and contact details
Contact information using free or suspicious email domains
Multiple spelling or grammatical errors in business-context emails
detection_criteria: Flag emails with >1 suspicious URL or URLs with uncommon TLDs
Flag subject lines containing monetary values or urgent phrases
Flag emails with body length >500 words containing financial scam narratives
Flag presence of free or public email addresses in contact info within financial or health contexts
Flag emails with >3 spelling or grammatical errors in professional communication
normal_vs_malicious: Benign emails have professional or neutral subject lines without monetary inducements
Legitimate URLs correspond to known reputable domains matching sender source
Normal email bodies are coherent, topic-consistent, and free of unsolicited financial offers
Legitimate contact info aligns with sender domain and organizational context
Minimal spelling and grammatical errors in professional emails
measurable_thresholds: More than one suspicious URL per email triggers suspicion
Subject lines containing '$' or urgent keywords raise alerts
Body length exceeding 500 words with scam keywords is suspicious
Contact emails from free providers in sensitive contexts are flagged
More than three spelling/grammar errors in professional emails indicate risk

attack_scenarios: An email claiming to be from a senior credit officer detailing an abandoned sum of 12.5 million British pounds, requesting cooperation and including free email contact info and obfuscated URLs.
A phishing email promoting an online pharmacy with a direct suspicious URL, claiming FDA approval and offering discounts on medications.
A short spam-like email listing cheap medications with embedded suspicious URLs using uncommon TLDs and numeric strings.
legitimate_scenarios: A business email with a neutral subject line related to a quarterly report, containing structured, coherent text and URLs matching the sender's domain.
An academic newsletter email with formal salutations, consistent organizational signatures, and no unsolicited financial offers or suspicious links.
A transactional email from a known vendor with professional formatting, legitimate contact information, and links to reputable domains.

risk_reduction: Implement email filtering with URL reputation and domain age verification for embedded links.
Apply content-based detection using natural language processing to identify social engineering narratives and phishing keywords.
Enforce sender authentication protocols (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) to verify sender domain consistency.
Deploy heuristic analysis to flag emails with multiple suspicious URLs, monetary inducements, and free email contact addresses.
Continuously monitor for repeated phishing keywords and suspicious domain patterns to update blacklists and detection models.

key_features_to_vary: Email subject lines with varying urgency and monetary inducements
Body length from short spam-like to long narrative scams
URL domain characteristics including TLDs, obfuscation, and registration age
Presence and style of contact information including free and suspicious email domains
Language style variations: formal, informal, spam-like with misspellings
pattern_preservation: Maintain narrative-rich scam structures with detailed backstories
Preserve use of obfuscated or shortened URLs with uncommon TLDs
Include social engineering tactics appealing to urgency and emotion
Embed typical phishing keywords and financial or health-related themes
realism_requirements: Ensure linguistic diversity reflecting multi-source email origins
Incorporate realistic sender metadata consistent with email content
Balance class distribution to reflect real-world benign and malicious ratios
Simulate common formatting and grammatical error patterns observed in attacks
diversity_dimensions: Vary sender domains and source identifiers to simulate multi-source data
Include different phishing themes such as financial scams, health products, and job offers
Generate emails with different body lengths and complexity
Vary URL obfuscation techniques and domain registration ages
Simulate both professional and spam-like language styles
